questions.text: Under the Architect's Code of Ethical Conduct, which statement regarding injurious conduct is accurate?

options.text: Only knowingly false statements constitute prohibited injurious conduct; truthful statements are always permissible, provided they are made in good faith
Truthful statements about a competitor's prior errors represent legitimate professional discussion; false or exaggerated statements constitute prohibited injurious conduct
Any negative statement about a competitor's professional reputation violates Rule 7.5, regardless of truth, as it may harm professional relationships
Injurious conduct applies only to public statements; private criticism is not covered, unless it is shared beyond the intended private audience

rationale.a: While false statements are prohibited, truthful statements about errors are permissible; the standard is not absolute prohibition of all negative commentary. [cite: 582]
rationale.c: The prohibition covers false or exaggerated statements, not all negative statements; truthful professional discussion is permitted. [cite: 582]
rationale.d: Rule 7.5 applies to conduct that injures reputation, prospects, or practice; the scope extends beyond only public statements. [cite: 523, 569]
rationale.correct: Rule 7.5 (formerly Section 5-g) prohibits 'maliciously, directly or indirectly' injuring the professional reputation of another architect. Truthful professional evaluation is permitted, but false or exaggerated claims are prohibited. [cite: 523, 569, 582]
rationale.takeaway: Rule 7.5 prohibits false or malicious statements; truthful professional discussion about competitor errors is permitted for legitimate review. [cite: 523, 582]

questions.code_citation: Code of Ethical Conduct, Article VI, Rule 7.5; RA 9266 Section 23

questions.text: An architect discovers that the original designer of a building renovation is still actively practicing. Which sequence of actions best satisfies the Code's takeover obligations?

options.text: Accept the owner's preference, notify the original architect afterward, and request confirmation of employment termination, ensuring all parties are informed
Decline the project entirely rather than contact the competing architect, avoiding any potential conflict of interest
Contact the original architect in writing, request documentation of employment termination with the owner, and confirm compensation settlement before proceeding
Proceed with the project since the owner clearly intends to change architects, satisfying the requirement without further action

rationale.a: Notification after acceptance does not satisfy the sequential requirement; notification must precede engagement assumption. [cite: 550]
rationale.b: Declining is not required; the architect must follow the Rule 7.3 sequence to determine if the engagement is permissible. [cite: 550]
rationale.d: Owner preference does not satisfy the formal Rule 7.3 requirements; the architect must execute the proper notification and documentation sequence. [cite: 550]
rationale.correct: Rule 7.3 requires written notification first, then conclusive determination of employment termination, and finally verification of compensation completion. [cite: 523, 535, 550]
rationale.takeaway: Rule 7.3 requires formal written notification to the original architect with documented termination and compensation verification before engagement. [cite: 550]

questions.code_citation: Code of Ethical Conduct, Article VI, Rule 7.3; RA 9266 Section 23

questions.text: An architect performs 35% of renovation work on a structure where 65% of the original design remains in place. A client asks the architect to claim equal design credit in marketing materials. What should the architect do?

options.text: Grant the request since the renovation work is substantial enough to justify equal credit
Claim primary credit for the renovation work while acknowledging the original design exists
Decline the request and limit public marketing to the 35% contribution actually performed
Claim ownership of the original design percentage if the original architect cannot be located

rationale.a: Substantial renovation work does not justify equal credit; proportional credit assignment is the mandatory standard under Rule 7.4. [cite: 582]
rationale.b: Primary credit cannot be claimed for minority contribution; the percentage of work performed determines credit limitations. [cite: 582]
rationale.d: Inability to locate a predecessor does not permit ownership claims of their work; this would be a direct violation of Rule 7.4. [cite: 533]
rationale.correct: Rule 7.4 requires that credit match actual contribution. Claiming equal credit when only performing 35% of the work violates the requirement for proportional credit assignment. [cite: 533, 582]
rationale.takeaway: Credit claims must match actual contribution percentage; substantial work does not justify primary or equal credit with the original designer. [cite: 582]

questions.code_citation: Code of Ethical Conduct, Article VI, Rule 7.4; RA 9266 Section 23

questions.text: An architect is designing additions to a historic building originally designed by a colleague. Under Article VI, Rule 7.4, what credit may the architect claim if 75% of the original floor area remains unchanged?

options.text: The architect may claim primary design credit since the project received substantial new additions
The architect may claim equal partnership credit with the original designer for the entire project
The architect must limit public claims to only the 25% of work actually new or substantially modified
The architect may omit mention of the original architect to avoid confusion among clients

rationale.a: Substantial original design retention requires proportional credit limitation, not a primary credit claim. [cite: 582]
rationale.b: Rule 7.4 prohibits claiming the works of others as one's own; credit must be proportional to actual contribution. [cite: 582]
rationale.d: The Code requires honoring the work of other architects; omission of a predecessor's credit violates professional ethical standards. [cite: 523, 533]
rationale.correct: Rule 7.4 (formerly Section 5-f) states: 'Credit shall only be for the specific work he has done.' With 75% of the original design maintained, credit is limited to the 25% new work performed. [cite: 533, 582]
rationale.takeaway: Credit claims must be proportional to actual contribution; an architect cannot claim work done by a predecessor. [cite: 533, 582]

questions.code_citation: Code of Ethical Conduct, Article VI, Rule 7.4; RA 9266 Section 23

questions.text: An architect completes 40% of a renovation project. Marketing materials on the firm's website describe 'our design approach' for the entire building without specifically mentioning the original architect. Is this a violation?

options.text: No violation occurred; the owner's satisfaction demonstrates compliance with professional standards, as long as the client agrees
Yes, because proportional credit assignment requires specifying the architect's 40% contribution and distinguishing the original work
No violation because the architect performed substantial work exceeding 25% of the project, which is a common industry threshold
Violation occurs only if the original architect objects to the marketing language used, which is rare

rationale.a: Client satisfaction does not override ethical requirements; credit representation must align with actual contribution regardless of satisfaction. [cite: 582]
rationale.c: Substantial work does not eliminate the requirement for proportional credit assignment; the contribution must be accurately represented. [cite: 582]
rationale.d: The violation occurs through the misrepresentation itself; a predecessor's objection is not required to establish a violation of Rule 7.4. [cite: 582]
rationale.correct: Rule 7.4 states that an architect must not claim the works of another as his own. Marketing language that implies responsibility for the entire building violates the requirement for proportional credit assignment. [cite: 533, 582]
rationale.takeaway: Marketing language must clearly reflect proportional contribution; using 'our design' for work done by others violates credit attribution requirements. [cite: 582]

questions.code_citation: Code of Ethical Conduct, Article VI, Rule 7.4; RA 9266 Section 23

questions.text: Under the Architect's Code of Ethical Conduct (Article VI), when may an architect pursue a commission previously offered to another architect?

options.text: Immediately, since the competing architect may decline the work, and the client may prefer a different approach
The prohibition is absolute; the architect cannot pursue such a commission under any circumstances
Only if the original architect has been practicing fewer than five years and lacks the necessary experience
After notifying the competing architect verbally of intent to pursue the work, and ensuring no conflict of interest exists

rationale.a: The Code does not permit immediate pursuit based on potential declination; the prohibition covers all methods and circumstances. [cite: 535]
rationale.c: Duration of prior practice does not create an exception to the non-poaching prohibition. [cite: 535]
rationale.d: Verbal notification does not satisfy or overcome the absolute prohibition established by Rule 7.1. [cite: 535]
rationale.correct: Rule 7.1 (formerly Section 5-c) establishes an absolute prohibition on seeking commissions previously endowed to another architect. The Code states: 'He shall not seek a commission on which another Architect has been or is being employed.' [cite: 522, 535]
rationale.takeaway: Non-poaching under the Code is an absolute prohibition with no exceptions based on circumstances or architect tenure. [cite: 535]

questions.code_citation: Code of Ethical Conduct, Article VI, Rule 7.1; RA 9266 Section 23

questions.text: Regarding the 'takeover' of a project, what is the critical difference between notification and the complete Rule 7.3 obligation?

options.text: Notification is synonymous with the complete obligation; there is no additional requirement, as the process is considered fulfilled upon initial communication
Notification is the first step, but Rule 7.3 also demands determination of employment termination and verification of compensation completion
Notification satisfies the requirement only if delivered by certified mail, ensuring receipt by the intended party
Notification is sufficient if delivered to the original architect's last known address, provided it is accompanied by a formal acknowledgment of receipt

rationale.a: The Code refutes this; notification is the first step, not the entire obligation. [cite: 550]
rationale.c: The method of delivery is not the defining factor; the execution of all three sequential steps is what fulfills the obligation. [cite: 550]
rationale.d: Delivery does not complete the obligation; verification of termination and compensation completion remain required. [cite: 550]
rationale.correct: Notification is only the first of three sequential steps mandated by Rule 7.3. The architect must also verify the predecessor's contract has been terminated and that they have been paid for services. [cite: 523, 535, 550]
rationale.takeaway: Rule 7.3's three sequential steps must be fully executed; notification is merely the first of three required confirmations. [cite: 550]

questions.code_citation: Code of Ethical Conduct, Article VI, Rule 7.3; RA 9266 Section 23

questions.text: An architect is approached to design a major renovation of a 1905 landmark building. The original architect is deceased. According to Article VI, Rule 7.4, what is the architect's obligation?

options.text: The architect may proceed since the original architect is deceased and the obligation cannot be fulfilled, allowing for creative freedom
The architect must still preserve or restore as much of the original design as possible and document the effort to identify the original designer's estate
The architect should modify substantial portions of the original design to demonstrate independent contribution, showcasing their own design philosophy
The obligation to notify applies only when the original architect is living and actively practicing, ensuring respect for the original creator's ongoing work

rationale.a: Deceased status does not eliminate the preservation obligation; cultural stewardship continues as a professional duty. [cite: 570]
rationale.c: Preservation is required; extensive modification for the sake of demonstrating independent contribution violates the heritage preservation duty. [cite: 570, 582]
rationale.d: The preservation obligation extends to the work itself and the predecessor's legacy as part of professional stewardship. [cite: 570]
rationale.correct: Rule 7.4 emphasizes architectural heritage preservation: 'he shall... preserve or restore as much of the original design as possible.' This professional stewardship obligation applies regardless of whether the original architect is living. [cite: 570, 582]
rationale.takeaway: Heritage preservation obligation continues beyond the original architect's lifetime; conservation of design elements is a professional duty. [cite: 570, 582]

questions.code_citation: Code of Ethical Conduct, Article VI, Rule 7.4; RA 9266 Section 23

questions.text: An architect learns that a competitor designed a building renovation 20 years ago, but the original architect is now retired. What must the architect do before accepting a new commission for the same building?

options.text: Proceed with the design since the original architect is retired and unavailable, assuming no further obligations
The architect must still attempt to notify the original architect and determine their engagement status
Notify only the current property owner and disclose the original architect's identity in marketing, ensuring transparency
Conduct only routine maintenance work to avoid any obligation to the original designer, minimizing potential conflicts

rationale.a: Retirement status does not eliminate the notification obligation or prior design involvement responsibility. [cite: 535]
rationale.c: Owner notification alone does not satisfy Rule 7.3; the original architect must be notified directly. [cite: 535]
rationale.d: The scope of work does not eliminate the ethical obligation to research and notify regarding prior design involvement. [cite: 535]
rationale.correct: Rule 7.3 and Rule 7.4 apply to any prior design involvement. Retirement does not extinguish the obligation to attempt notification and verify termination of the previous professional relationship. [cite: 523, 535]
rationale.takeaway: Code obligations to prior architects persist regardless of time elapsed or retirement status. [cite: 535]

questions.code_citation: Code of Ethical Conduct, Article VI, Rule 7.3; RA 9266 Section 23

questions.text: The Code of Ethical Conduct requires three sequential confirmations before an architect may assume engagement on a project previously handled by another architect. Which sequence is correct?

options.text: Verify termination, notify original architect, confirm compensation completion, ensuring all contractual obligations are met
Confirm compensation completion, written notification, verify termination, and ensure all parties are informed
Written notification to the original architect, conclusive determination of employment termination, and verification of compensation completion
Notify client of prior architect's work, request original architect's written permission, complete the engagement, and ensure compliance with ethical standards

rationale.a: Verification cannot precede notification; written notice must be initiated first according to Rule 7.3. [cite: 550]
rationale.b: The sequence omits the critical element of conclusively determining employment termination and places compensation completion first. [cite: 550]
rationale.d: Rule 7.3 requires actions involving the original architect directly, not just client notification or simple 'permission.' [cite: 535]
rationale.correct: Rule 7.3 (formerly Section 5-e) requires a sequential process: notification first, then verification of termination, then proof of compensation completion. [cite: 523, 535, 550]
rationale.takeaway: Rule 7.3 imposes three sequential steps in order: written notification, employment termination verification, and compensation settlement confirmation. [cite: 550]
